# Animals and humans (alternate voice)

::: {.callout-important}
## This is a voice comparison, not a chapter
Same content, same citations, same evidence as
[Animals and humans](../chapters/02-animals.qmd). Only the writing differs.
Two things vary together here: the collective "we", and a more argumentative
pace. One of these will be kept and this page deleted.
:::

Almost every human gene is alternatively spliced, and on its own that fact
settles nothing. A gene can make twenty transcripts that all do the same job,
and a gene can make two that do opposite jobs. So we build this chapter out of
cases where someone tied an isoform difference to a phenotype, because those are
the only cases that carry weight.

## Dscam1: diversity by combination {#sec-dscam-we}

If you want one gene to make the case, use *Drosophila* *Dscam1*. Nothing else
is this extreme, and nothing else has been taken apart this thoroughly.

Start with the architecture, which multiplies rather than adds. Three clusters
of mutually exclusive exons hold 12, 48 and 33 variants, and splicing picks
exactly one from each. That gives 19,008 ectodomains, and an alternative
transmembrane exon doubles it to the 38,016 everyone quotes
[@dong2023dscamscreen].

![Three mutually exclusive exon clusters and one alternative transmembrane exon
generate the *Dscam1* repertoire. A single neuron uses a small, probabilistically
drawn slice of it.](../figures/dscam-combinatorics.svg){#fig-dscam-we width=100%}

We belabour the arithmetic because the number usually gets quoted as a curiosity
about how far splicing can be pushed. It is better read as a specification. Each
Dscam1 ectodomain binds homophilically with near-absolute specificity: an isoform
recognises itself and barely touches the others [@dscam2004homophilicbinding].
That makes an isoform a usable identity label, and the repertoire size tells you
how many distinguishable labels the animal has to work with.

The label is used for repulsion. Sister dendrites of one neuron carry matching
isoforms, recognise each other and turn away; branches of different neurons pass
without incident. Recognition happens in the variable ectodomain, but the
cytoplasmic tail does the repelling [@dscam2007dendriteselfavoidance]. Notice
what this implies. Self-avoidance needs a neuron's isoform set to be
*distinctive*, not to be any *particular* set. And that is exactly what we see:
R3/R4 photoreceptors express something like 14 to 50 distinct isoform mRNAs each
[@dscam2004stochasticbiased], a vanishing slice of the repertoire.

How does a cell pick one variant per cluster? In *cis*, by RNA structure, with no
trans-acting factor adjudicating. One intronic docking site pairs with the
selector sequence upstream of a single variable exon, physically presenting that
exon and no other to the upstream constitutive exon [@dscam2005dockingselector].

### How much diversity is required

Two experiments take us from correlation to requirement.

First, alleles cutting the maximum repertoire from 38,016 to 22,176 still caused
specific connectivity defects in mechanosensory neurons
[@dscam2006diversityrequired]. The number itself is under selection.

Second, and more informative, a CRISPR deletion series spanning 396 to 18,612
possible ectodomains showed there is no single requirement to measure. Dendrite
self/non-self discrimination saturated around 2,000 isoforms and did not care
which cluster supplied them. Axon patterning needed far more, and depended on
which clusters were present [@dong2023dscamscreen]. We read this as diversity
doing two jobs in two different currencies: one wants a sufficient count, the
other wants particular identities.

### Bias, and a crack in the standard model

Isoform usage is skewed, and the skew does work. Flies with normal Dscam1 protein
levels and an unchanged number of possible isoforms, but a shifted exon 9 usage
distribution, showed marked mushroom-body defects. The same shift at exon 4 did
nothing [@dscam2021splicingbias]. Changing bias damaged axonal wiring while
leaving the self-avoidance of axonal branches intact, which is precisely the
function the isoform count is supposed to underwrite [@dscam2021splicingbias].

Those authors see the problem their own result creates, and say so: heavy,
reproducible bias restricts access to the diversity that self-avoidance is
supposed to exploit [@hong2019dscamsplicingbias]. We have no resolution to offer
and we are not going to paper over it.

## Splicing as a developmental switch

*Dscam1* uses splicing to generate variety. The *Drosophila* sex-determination
cascade uses it to make a decision, and it is still the cleanest example of a
splicing switch running a developmental programme.

The cascade is a chain of splice choices. Female Sex-lethal binds the
*transformer* transcript at or near its non-sex-specific 3' acceptor, forcing the
downstream female-productive acceptor instead [@sxl1990trasplicesite]. At the
bottom, Tra and Tra2 work positively, pulling SR-family factors onto an element
downstream of the female-specific 3' splice site of *doublesex*, and that complex
commits the pre-mRNA [@dsx1993spliceenhancercomplex].

*doublesex* also gives us the cleanest two-isoforms-opposite-jobs case anywhere.
The female product represses male differentiation; the male product represses
female differentiation. Same primary transcript, both products functional
[@dsx1989sexspecificpolypeptides].

## Isoform switching within a cell's lifetime

Developmental cascades set an isoform once and move on. CD45 shows the same
machinery running reversibly, as routine immune function.

Human CD45 makes five transmembrane phosphatase isoforms differing only in their
extracellular domains, by including or skipping variable exons 4, 5 and 6.
Resting T cells carry long forms keeping two or three of those exons; activated T
cells drop most or all of them [@cd452005variableexonelements]. Length matters.
In T cell lines with a defined receptor, the short exon-null isoform typical of
memory CD4 cells supported antigen recognition best
[@cd451994isoformsrecognition]. The splice choice tunes signalling sensitivity
and leaves receptor specificity alone.

## Opposing functions from one gene

The *bcl-x* locus was described from the start as making two products that pull
against each other, with the short form actively opposing bcl-2 rather than
merely failing to protect cells [@bclx1993dominantregulator].

The structure explains the reversal. Bcl-xS is missing 63 amino acids spanning
BH1 and BH2, the stretch that makes Bcl-xL look most like Bcl-2. The mechanism is
shakier than the antagonism, and we want to be careful here. The original work
found Bcl-xS binding Bcl-xL only weakly in vitro, saw no heterodimers in cells,
and argued the mechanism therefore differs from other pro-apoptotic family
members [@bclx1996santagonizesl]. A 2019 review states it as direct inhibition,
with Bcl-xS binding Bcl-xL and Bcl-2 and releasing Bak [@stevens2019bclxsplicing].
We take the antagonism as settled and the heterodimer model as resting on the
review, not the primary report.

## Isoforms that set tissue mechanics

Titin is the case where a spliced product's physical properties simply are the
phenotype. The adult human heart runs a long compliant N2BA form of roughly 3,200
to 3,500 kDa alongside a short stiff N2B form near 3,000 kDa, both from one gene
of 364 exons [@li2022rbm20titinstiffness]. The difference comes down to how much
extensible material survives splicing: the compliant form keeps more PEVK and
immunoglobulin-like spring elements in the I-band.

One factor sets the ratio. RBM20 is the principal regulator of titin pre-mRNA,
and losing a single functional copy pushes splicing toward highly compliant
isoforms and degrades the Frank-Starling response [@li2022rbm20titinstiffness].

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why a spliced-out segment changes stiffness

Titin spans half a sarcomere and sits in series with the contractile machinery
like a spring. Its I-band region holds tandem immunoglobulin-like domains that
unfold under load, plus a PEVK segment that behaves as an entropic spring. Keep
more of those elements and you lengthen the spring, so the same stretch gives
less restoring force. Splicing is not tuning an activity here. It is changing how
much polymer sits between two anchors.
:::

## Ligand specificity by mutually exclusive exon

In FGFR1 through FGFR3, the mutually exclusive IIIb and IIIc exons encode the
C-terminal half of immunoglobulin loop III, which sits in the ligand-binding
site. The splice choice decides which fibroblast growth factors the receptor can
answer to at all [@holzmann2011fgfrigiiisplicing].

They are not interchangeable. Deleting IIIb in mouse is lethal; deleting IIIc
gives skeletal malformations instead [@holzmann2011fgfrigiiisplicing]. Usage
splits by compartment, IIIb in epithelia and IIIc in mesenchyme, and a
IIIb-to-IIIc switch in an epithelial tumour tracks with invasiveness in bladder
and prostate cancer [@holzmann2011fgfrigiiisplicing].

## A cautionary case: PKM1 and PKM2

Pyruvate kinase M is the textbook illustration of how much can ride on one
mutually exclusive exon pair. It is also our best illustration of an isoform
story outrunning its evidence, which is why we include it.

Antisense oligonucleotides blocking an exon 10 enhancer, forcing exon 9
inclusion, killed glioblastoma cells, and the authors pinned the death on loss of
PK-M2 rather than gain of PK-M1 [@wang2012pkmantisense]. Force the splice choice
and you get a large phenotype. That much is solid.

The familiar version goes further and says tumours switch from PKM1 to PKM2.
Absolute mass spectrometry across 25 human cancers with tissue-matched controls
found PKM2 predominant in tumours and equally predominant in the matched normal
tissue, and those authors reject the switch outright [@bluemlein2011pkmnoshift].
We will say that forcing the choice has a phenotype. We will not say that tumours
make the switch.

## How much of this is functional

Three bodies of evidence speak to whether most alternative splicing looks like
the cases above. They disagree, and we think the disagreement is the finding.

**Tissue regulation is extensive.** The 2008 tissue survey found over 22,000
tissue-specific alternative transcript events and estimated that 52 to 80 per
cent of events of each type are tissue-regulated [@wang2008alternative]. The
exons switching hardest between tissues were also likeliest to preserve reading
frame in both isoforms, which those authors read as splicing making two intact
proteins rather than switching a gene off [@wang2008alternative].

**Most of the catalogue is not conserved.** A human-mouse comparison predicted
only about 2,000 conserved alternatively spliced exons, found them markedly more
frame-preserving and domain-sparing than the rest, and concluded that the great
majority of human EST-record alternative splicing has no mouse counterpart
[@conservedas2005humanmouseexons]. The same split shows up in worms: in *C.
elegans*, tissue-differential splicing events are preferentially frame-preserving
and better conserved across *Caenorhabditis* than other alternative exons
[@koterniak2020celegansplicing].

**A real fraction is error, and another fraction is neither error nor protein
diversity.** De novo junction discovery turned up about 150,000 unannotated
junctions in human cells, with little conservation at the new splice sites and an
implied error rate near 0.7 per cent per intron, lower in highly expressed genes
[@pickrell2010noisysplicing]. Meanwhile one transcript usually dominates: about
85 per cent of protein-coding mRNA in primary tissues came from each gene's major
transcript, though roughly 35 per cent of genes switch which transcript dominates
between tissues, and those authors pointedly declined to call minor transcripts
functionless [@gonzalezporta2013dominanttranscript].

A third position reframes the question entirely. Measuring unproductive splicing
across eight assays gave threefold more of it than steady-state RNA suggested,
with 15 per cent of transcript molecules from protein-coding genes unproductive,
and trait-associated loci acting through splicing were as often explained by
decay-driven expression changes as by isoform usage
[@fair2024unproductivesplicing]. On that reading, much alternative splicing is
neither protein diversity nor noise. It is a volume knob.

These results fit together once you stop expecting a single answer. Most splicing
events are rare, unconserved and probably inconsequential. A minority are
switch-like, frame-preserving and conserved. A further portion sets expression
level through decay. Everything earlier in this chapter comes from the second
group, and we want to be explicit that nothing here licenses treating every
annotated isoform as a functional entity.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What the "95 per cent" figure actually counts

Two 2008 papers put alternative splicing at roughly 95 per cent of human
multi-exon genes, and the number now circulates stripped of its conditions.

Extrapolating by read coverage gave about 98 per cent of multi-exon genes
excluding cell lines, and about 100 per cent using everything. Require a minor
isoform to hit 15 per cent frequency in at least one sample and it drops to 92
per cent of multi-exon genes, or about 86 per cent of all human genes
[@wang2008alternative]. The independent survey got roughly 95 per cent of
multi-exon genes by a different route, and counted about 100,000 intermediate- to
high-abundance splicing events in major tissues [@pan2008deepsurveying].

Three things move between those statements: multi-exon genes or all genes as the
denominator, what abundance threshold a minor isoform must clear, and whether
detection is direct or extrapolated. Quote "95 per cent" without them and you
have said something uninterpretable rather than something wrong.
:::
